article.overview: A cable deployment system is a payload that lays out a cable or tether across the lunar surface, usually from a robot, rover or lander, and may also control the tension of the cable, reel it back in and carry electrical power or data through it. Such a system would let power or communications be moved from one point to another without building a fixed route. Among the payload types in this catalogue it is a deployment and infrastructure technology rather than a scientific instrument. The best-documented example reviewed is Astrobotic Technology's LunaGrid-Lite (LGL). It is a NASA-industry partnership demonstration in which a robotic cable deployer carried by a small CubeRover would unreel a long cable and send power through it. At the time of the most recent primary source reviewed (August 2025), LGL had passed Critical Design Review and was building flight hardware. No launch had been confirmed in the sources found [1][2][4].
article.description: A cable deployment system combines three functions. (1) Storage and payout: a cable is wound on a reel or spool, and a motor, brake or other mechanism releases it in a controlled way as the carrier moves away from the reel. The LGL reel is described in secondary material as housing the power cable and a tensioning/reverse mechanism; this was not confirmed in primary text [7]. (2) Tension and handling: the cable must be kept taut enough to avoid tangling or snagging, but not so taut that it damages itself or the carrier. Lunar terrain such as regolith and rock can abrade or catch the cable. (3) Transmission: the cable carries electrical power, and possibly data, between two ends. In LGL, the target is power from a lander to a rover at the end of the cable [1][3][4]. The payload name describes a function, not a single design. Documented concepts include a self-contained robotic cable deployer [4], a crane with a cable-management system [5] and a rover tether with an internal spool [6]. These share the problem of controlled payout of a long flexible line on an uneven surface, but differ substantially in mass, scale, power and purpose.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of this payload class is to provide a tethered connection on the lunar surface. Power distribution: NASA describes the LGL demonstration as advancing 'power generation and distribution technologies' [1][2]. Astrobotic describes it as the first transmission of power between assets on the Moon and the first high-voltage power transmitted through a cable across the lunar surface; these are planned claims, not results [3][4]. Tethered mobility and access: the JPL Moon Diver concept proposes a tethered rover that would pay out a tether to descend into a lunar pit and deploy instruments along its wall; the tether would supply power and communications and provide mechanical support [6]. Cable-based lifting: the ESA Loader crane uses a cable-management system to keep a compact crane controllable during deployment and to place cargo up to a few metres from a lander [5]. No peer-reviewed scientific results from a lunar cable deployment system were found in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: A cable deployment system uses a reel or spool, a payout mechanism and a carrier that moves the far end of the cable. In the LGL plan, a CubeRover with an integrated robotic cable deployer unreels the cable while moving [4]. The cable connects to a power source at the lander and a load at the rover or work site [1][3]. The JPL tether design uses an internal spool in the rover, which pays out the tether as the rover moves [6]. The ESA crane is different in kind: it is folded on the lander deck, unfolds after landing, and uses a cable-management system to control its arm while it lifts and places cargo [5]. Transmitting high power through a long cable on the Moon depends on voltage, frequency, cable losses and power-conversion equipment. The 2024 Astrobotic demonstration reports lab measurements of power factor, cable efficiency and voltage drop on spooled and unspooled cable, but the source gives no numeric values for those quantities [3].
article.scientific_importance: The scientific importance of this payload class is indirect. It does not measure the Moon's properties itself. Its importance lies in enabling power and data links to instruments, habitats or surface assets that cannot be placed next to a single lander, and in creating operational experience with long lunar cables. These capabilities would support longer-term surface science and infrastructure, but the reviewed sources do not quantify that benefit for any specific science mission.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a cable deployment system. Cable length, mass, power and mechanism depend on the mission. The three examples are described separately because they are not directly comparable: one is a power demonstration, one is a crane, and one is a rover tether concept. No comparison table is used because the values do not share the same measurement basis.

examples.name: LunaGrid-Lite (LGL) cable deployment and power transmission demonstration
examples.type: Planned NASA-industry partnership demonstration by Astrobotic Technology
examples.flight_status: Not flown in the sources reviewed. Critical Design Review passed and flight hardware in build as of August 2025.
examples.mass_statement: Not publicly specified in primary sources. Astrobotic describes the cable as 'ultra-light' and the converter as 'low mass' without figures [4]. A secondary summary of a 2024 JHU/APL slide deck mentions a total system mass of about 20 kg; not verified against the slide deck text [7].
cable_length_statements: NASA 2023 Tipping Point selection: 'the robotic deployment of one kilometer of cable' [1].
Astrobotic, 19 July 2024: an Astrobotic CubeRover 'will unreel 1 kilometer of cable' in the planned mission [3].
Astrobotic, 20 August 2025: LGL 'will deploy 500m of ultra-light cable' [4].
NASA power technology page, last updated 29 July 2026: 'long-distance (100 m – 500 m), high power (1 kW)' transmission [2].
power_statements: Target: 1 kW of power transmitted on the Moon. Planned demonstration, not an achieved result [2][4].
Laboratory test reported 19 July 2024: '1kW of alternating current (AC) power' transmitted through '1,000ft' (about 305 m) of ultra-light cable. Lab result, not a lunar measurement [3].
The 2024 release describes 1 kV and 1 kHz as the 'desired' transmission voltage and frequency; these are design targets in the source, not confirmed test values [3].
examples.deployment_system: Astrobotic's 2025 release describes the first 4U CubeRover 'integrated with the robotic cable deployer' [4]. NASA's 2023 page says the work covers 'a high-voltage power converter, cable, and cable reel system' and that a CubeRover will deploy the power line [1]. The reel's internal design is not described in primary text reviewed.
examples.dimensions_and_cable_diameter: Not publicly specified in primary sources reviewed.

examples.name: ESA Loader lunar crane
examples.type: ESA technology development project (related cable-managed deployment example; not a cable-payout power or data system)
examples.flight_status: Scaled laboratory model tested at ESA's Planetary Robotics Laboratory. No full-size unit is described as flown.
examples.dimensions_statement: The full-size crane is described as more than twice the size of the model; no numeric dimensions or crane mass are given [5].
examples.deployment: Launched folded on the lander payload deck and deployed after landing. The page describes a dedicated cable-management system and a defined unfolding sequence, without detailing the mechanism. Includes a levelling system and a two-joint arm ending in a passive spring-loaded gripper and a battery-powered rotating gripper [5].
examples.interface_statement: The source associates the crane with ESA's Argonaut lunar lander, which can deliver up to 1,500 kg of cargo. This is an association stated on the ESA page, not a verified interface specification [5].

examples.name: JPL Moon Diver rover tether concept
examples.type: Proposed concept with prototype tests (no flight described)
examples.flight_status: Proposed Moon Diver mission concept; prototype tests described in the paper. No flight.
examples.payout_mechanism: The rover 'pays out tether from an internal spool'. Respooling is not described in the reviewed abstract.
examples.diameter_and_strength: Not publicly specified in the reviewed abstract; full text not accessed.
examples.environment: The tether must survive abrasion from 'glassy regolith and volcanic rocks', thermal extremes and UV exposure, and must contact terrain while under load [6].
examples.test_results: The paper describes mechanical, electrical and environmental prototype tests and lessons from lab and field tests. The reviewed abstract gives no quantitative deployment results.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single dimension set exists for this payload class. LGL dimensions and cable diameter are not publicly specified. The ESA crane's full-size dimensions are not given, only a statement that the full-size unit is more than twice the model. The JPL tether diameter is not specified in the reviewed abstract. The three examples should not be compared on dimensions.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for LGL cable, reel or converter in primary sources; a secondary summary's approximately 20 kg total system figure is unverified [7]. The ESA crane's mass is not given [5]. The JPL tether mass is not given in the reviewed abstract [6]. Mass affects launch requirements, lander capacity and deployment design, and cannot be assessed for any specific system from the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LGL targets 1 kW transmission [2][4] with a lab-test result of 1 kW AC through about 305 m of ultra-light cable [3]. The ESA crane's power requirement is not stated in the reviewed page [5]. The JPL tether is designed to carry up to 100 W of power and 1 Mbps of data [6]. These are targets or design envelopes and are not interchangeable.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar cable must operate in vacuum, with large temperature swings and ultraviolet exposure. The JPL concept lists abrasion, sharp edges, thermal extremes and UV exposure as design drivers [6]. Lunar regolith and rock abrasion are therefore a central design issue for any cable that lies on or drags over the ground [6]. Secondary material on the LGL programme identifies regolith intrusion into the deployment mechanism, cable breaking and cable tangling during payout as key constraints [7]; this is a reported risk, not a verified requirement. General engineering considerations include thermal control of electronics, mechanical protection of joints and reels, and avoiding cable loads that could damage the carrier or the lander interface. These are general considerations; the reviewed sources give no quantitative requirements for LGL or any other system.
article.limitations: The LGL 1 kW power transmission and 500 m deployment are described as targets; no achieved lunar result was found [2][4]. Cable length is unresolved across sources (1 km, 500 m and 100–500 m for the same programme). Mass and interface data are missing in primary sources. The lander association is unverified: NASA's 2023 page says a CubeRover is delivered by Astrobotic's Griffin lander, while search results reviewed disagree about which lander would carry LGL [1][7]. The ESA crane, JPL tether and LGL demonstration are not interchangeable and should not be compared directly.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A cable deployment system is a surface payload. It can be delivered as a self-contained rover-plus-deployer package, as in the LGL plan, or as a crane or tether system folded on or attached to a lander. Interface data for a named lander are not verified in the reviewed sources.
transportation_process: Integrate the reel, cable and carrier on Earth with the lander and rover interfaces.
Launch the lander on a launch vehicle; the launch vehicle for LGL is not identified in the reviewed sources.

Transfer to the Moon and land the lander. NASA's 2023 statement says a CubeRover delivered by Astrobotic's Griffin lander will deploy the power line [1]; this is not verified as a current configuration.
Release the CubeRover and robotic cable deployer; unreel the cable while the rover moves, with tension control [4][7].
Connect the cable to the lander-side power source and to the load at the far end [1][3].
Commission the link and measure power and cable performance; the 2024 lab measurements (power factor, efficiency, voltage drop) are the only performance measurements described [3].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LGL: CubeRover carrying a robotic cable deployer and reel [1][4]. JPL concept: rover with an internal spool paying out tether during traverse [6]. ESA crane: folded on the lander deck, unfolded after landing, with a cable-management system controlling the arm [5].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No lunar cable deployment system has been reported as flown in the sources reviewed. LGL was in flight-hardware build as of August 2025 with flight-ready status targeted for 2026 by Astrobotic; no launch is confirmed [4]. The JPL tether is a proposed concept with prototype tests [6]. The ESA crane has a published laboratory model [5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility is asserted. Interface, mounting-load and power-bus data for LGL or any other named lander were not found in primary sources. The Astrobotic Griffin lander (NASA 2023 statement [1]) and a Voyager Griffin-1 mission named in search results [7] differ; the reviewed sources do not settle which vehicle would carry LGL.

article.historical_significance: No lunar cable deployment system has been reported as flown in the sources reviewed. Its historical importance so far lies in demonstrating intent and development. NASA's 2023 Tipping Point selection of LGL described the work as a demonstration of robotic cable deployment and power transmission across the lunar surface [1]. The JPL tether concept dates from a 2020 preprint and describes prototype work on a rover tether for a proposed pit mission [6]. ESA's 2026 Loader crane is a related development with a published laboratory model [5]. The sources do not establish a historical lineage for lunar cable deployment systems, and no earlier flown example was identified.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flight heritage was identified; all described systems are concepts, prototypes, laboratory models or planned demonstrations. Cable length and CubeRover size differ across sources (1 km versus 500 m versus 100–500 m; 4U in the 2025 release versus 6U in a secondary summary that was not verified). A search summary stated that LGL cable is designed to resist regolith abrasion, but the fetched 2024 Astrobotic article does not mention regolith or abrasion; that claim is excluded. Secondary summaries gave 1 kV, 1 kHz and about 20 kg total system mass; these appear only in secondary material and are not treated as verified. The JHU/APL LSIC slide deck (27 June 2024) was downloaded but its text could not be extracted; statements attributed to it are secondary and unverified [7]. Cable mass, diameter, breaking strength, reel mass, converter efficiency, operational lifetime and deployment accuracy are not publicly specified in the reviewed sources. Student projects and a 2026 Berkeley project document appeared in search results; their contents were not verified and are not used.

data_quality_notes: Status: LunaGrid-Lite is a planned demonstration. The most recent primary LGL source reviewed is the Astrobotic press release of 20 August 2025 and the NASA power page updated 29 July 2026. No launch or flight status was confirmed as of 13 November 2026; check Astrobotic or NASA for current status.

Cable length conflict: NASA 2023 Tipping Point page says one kilometer; Astrobotic 2024 says 1 km planned unreel; Astrobotic 2025 says 500 m; NASA power page (2026) lists 100 m to 500 m. Left unresolved.
CubeRover size conflict: Astrobotic 2025 says 4U; a secondary search summary said 6U. The 6U figure was not verified and is not used.

Unverified secondary claims excluded or flagged: the 2024 JHU/APL LSIC slide deck (reel tensioning/reverse mechanism, approximately 20 kg total system mass, regolith and tangling constraints, 500 m length) was downloaded but its text could not be extracted; statements from it are marked secondary.
Excluded claim: a search summary stated the LGL cable is designed to withstand regolith abrasion; the fetched 2024 Astrobotic article does not mention regolith or abrasion.
Voltage and frequency: 1 kV and 1 kHz appear in the 2024 Astrobotic release only as 'desired' transmission parameters, not confirmed test values.

Lander association: the NASA 2023 page names Astrobotic's Griffin lander as the CubeRover carrier. A search summary indicated disagreement with Voyager's Griffin-1; this is unresolved and no compatibility is asserted.
Image rights: Astrobotic image credit and reuse terms are not stated on the source page. ESA licence is the ESA Standard Licence as stated on its page.
Image verification: both direct image URLs returned HTTP 200 with image/jpeg content types. Full-resolution download and rights were not separately checked.
Mass, dimensions, cable diameter, breaking strength, reel mass, converter efficiency, lifetime and deployment accuracy for LGL are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

ESA Loader crane is a related cable-managed deployment example, not a cable-payout power or data system. Its lab-model and full-size figures are as stated by ESA; no full-size mass or dimensions are given.
JPL tether figures (100 W, 1 Mbps, 300 m traverse) are design targets from a 2020 preprint abstract; full text not accessed; no flight.

Not used: a Berkeley 2026 PDF (PlatinumCapstone deployment cabling document) returned binary content that could not be read; student projects (University of Colorado team 10; Devpost entry) and the USPTO tether patent were seen only in search results and are not used.
Research_status booleans set conservatively: the technical specifications are not fully audited, and the full-resolution image downloads were not checked.
